CoT unfaithfulness concerns whether stated reasoning reflects actual computation; SCB concerns whether \emph{self-extracted formal constraints} mirror the model's answer distribution. Even if traces were perfectly faithful, self-extraction would still inherit the distributional bias---the constraint $P(\text{answer\_A})$ reflects vote share, not logical validity. The shuffle control (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}) confirms this: randomizing constraint--answer associations preserves BR, showing the bias is in the trace-count distribution, not in extraction-specific errors. However, if traces are unfaithful, the mirage may be worse than our measurements suggest, because constraints would reflect not the model's reasoning but its post-hoc rationalization.

Our results do not imply that neuro-symbolic methods are inherently flawed---they imply that \emph{self-extracted} constraints cannot provide independent verification. The key distinction is \emph{when} formalization occurs relative to answer generation. Specification-generation approaches (e.g., SatLM \citep{ye2024satlm}, Logic-LM \citep{pan2023logiclm}) formalize the problem \emph{before} generating candidate answers, avoiding the extraction bottleneck; SatLM's success confirms that the formal verification mechanism is sound when constraints are independently derived. Trace-extraction (this work) operates post-hoc on reasoning traces that already contain candidates, inheriting the distributional prior that generates SCB. When post-hoc verification is unavoidable, practitioners should employ external verifiers from a different architecture family (\S\ref{sec:cross-arch}) and use the diagnostic framework in \S\ref{sec:discussion} to assess feasibility before deployment. The SCB diagnostic toolkit (below) provides detailed computation methods and threshold recommendations.

1	Can symbolic verification via a provably sound solver improve Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning when constraints are self-extracted from the model's own traces? We find no evidence of improvement. We introduce Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), which extracts logical constraints from chain-of-thought traces and selects answers via weighted MAX-SAT. Despite Z3 validating 99\% of self-extracted constraints, SICA produces answers identical to majority voting on over 90\% of problems across six models (7B--32B) and three reasoning domains. No condition shows a significant positive effect after FDR control; four of six powered conditions confirm equivalence within $\pm$2\,pp (TOST), though ten conditions remain underpowered for effects below ${\sim}$2\,pp. We systematically diagnose the failure as \emph{symbolic confirmation bias}: self-extracted constraints track the model's majority answer (bias ratios $1.66$--$4.97\times$ across nine models, 7B to frontier). We identify the structural mechanism---under source-attribution scoring and empirical degeneration, SICA reduces to majority vote (Observation~1)---and the $M{\to}T{\to}A{\to}C$ Markov chain that bounds self-extracted information (Remark~1), advancing beyond \citet{huang2024selfcorrect}'s findings to formal self-verification. Twenty-seven training-free variants within the constraint-extraction paradigm fail due to a persistent independence-accuracy trade-off. Preliminary cross-architecture verification escapes the bias ($+6.67$\,pp on the weakest generator, $p < 0.001$). Three zero-cost diagnostics characterize failure modes across all 60 tested conditions within this paradigm.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
\label{sec:main-results}

\looseness=-1 Table~\ref{tab:main_results} reports accuracy across all non-degenerate self-extraction conditions sorted by SC baseline. No condition shows a significant SICA effect after FDR control (BH, $m{=}16$). Two conditions show nominally significant degradation: Mistral-7B on ProofWriter ($-2.83$\,pp, raw $p = 0.014$) and Qwen2.5-14B on ProofWriter ($-2.50$\,pp, raw $p = 0.011$); both reach adjusted $p = 0.112$. An aggregate sign test yields 8 positive and 7 negative $\Delta$ values ($p = 1.00$, two-sided). When SICA and SC disagree, SC selects the correct answer $2.6\times$ more often (139 vs.\ 53 across conditions), indicating that constraint-based reweighting introduces noise rather than corrective signal.

\looseness=-1 Figure~\ref{fig:regime-scatter} reveals the regime structure underlying these results. Fleiss' $\kappa$ ranges from 0.21 to 0.82 across conditions, yielding $K_{\text{eff}} = 1.20\text{--}3.62$ at $K = 12$ (Table~\ref{tab:independence}, Appendix). Positive $\Delta$ requires both sufficient $K_{\text{eff}}$ ($\leq 1.30$ never improves) and reasonable SC accuracy ($K_{\text{eff}} = 3.62$ with SC $= 39\%$ degrades rather than helps). Three regimes emerge: Type~C (SC $\leq 40\%$), where low base accuracy causes error amplification; an intermediate band (50--60\%), containing the only positive trends; and Type~A (SC $\geq 60\%$), where symbolic confirmation bias dominates. Seed-level noise is substantial: across three Mistral-7B seeds, $\kappa \in [0.41, 0.51]$ yet $\Delta$ ranges from $+2.94$ to $-2.45$\,pp, indicating that constraint quality varies beyond what independence alone predicts. We trace the failure mechanism in \S\ref{sec:analysis}.

\looseness=-1 TOST equivalence tests \citep{lakens2017equivalence} with pre-specified margin $\pm 2$\,pp---based on the smallest meaningful SC gain reported in \citet{wang2023sc}---confirm four conditions as equivalent; ten remain underpowered for effects below ${\sim}2$\,pp (MDE 1.86--4.84\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:power}). TOST sensitivity analysis across three margins ($\pm 1$, $\pm 2$, $\pm 3$\,pp) confirms that equivalence conclusions are margin-dependent (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}). Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence for small effects. Three-seed replication on Mistral-7B confirms seed-level noise (mean $\Delta = +0.16 \pm 2.70$\,pp; Table~\ref{tab:multi-seed}). Four-seed replication on Qwen2.5-14B $\times$ FOLIO confirms the pattern ($\Delta \in [0.00, -2.01]$\,pp).

\looseness=-1 Oracle controls replacing self-extracted constraints with gold annotations confirm the MAX-SAT mechanism is sound ($+29.90$/$+13.73$\,pp FOLIO, $+17.17$\,pp ProofWriter; $p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only ${\sim}$12\% of this ceiling (Appendix~\ref{app:oracle}).

input.content: Can symbolic verification via a provably sound solver improve Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning when constraints are self-extracted from the model's own traces? We find no detectable improvement exceeding ${\sim}$2\,pp under self-extraction. We introduce Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), which extracts logical constraints from chain-of-thought traces via weighted MAX-SAT. Despite Z3 validating 99\% of self-extracted constraints, SICA produces answers identical to majority voting on over 90\% of problems across six models (7B--32B) and three domains. No condition shows a significant positive effect after FDR control; four of six powered conditions confirm equivalence within $\pm$2\,pp (TOST); the remainder are underpowered for smaller effects. The failure is structural: self-extracted constraints track the majority answer---a property we term \emph{symbolic confirmation bias} (bias ratios $1.66$--$4.97\times$ across nine models, 7B to frontier). Under source-attribution scoring and degeneration, SICA reduces to majority vote (Observation~1); the $M{\to}T{\to}A{\to}C$ Markov chain bounds self-extracted information (Remark~1), extending and formalizing \citet{huang2024selfcorrect}'s findings for formal self-verification. Twenty-seven training-free variants fail due to a persistent independence-accuracy trade-off. Cross-architecture verification escapes the bias ($+6.67$\,pp on the weakest generator, $p < 0.001$). Three zero-cost diagnostics characterize failure modes across all tested conditions.
